title: Compact Interop Toolkit blueprint + integration notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact blueprint for a lightweight Interop Toolkit aimed at decreasing friction when product teams integrate Redwood SDKs and the Redwood API into heterogeneous stacks. The goal is a small, opinionated distribution (CLI + templates + smoke harness + telemetry presets) that covers the 80%-onboard path for new internal and external integrators.

Constraints / Design tradeoffs:
- Keep core artifact < 5MB compressed (no heavy runtime dependencies).
- Language-agnostic surface: provide thin stubs and generated examples for core languages (JS/TS, Python, Go, Java).
- Offline-friendly dev loop: local emulator + deterministic fixture data for CI.
- Minimal cognitive load: one command to get a functioning sample app.

Key components: (compact set)
1) redwood-cli (dev only)
   - Commands: init, run-emulator, smoke, lint-prompts, bundle-samples
   - Intended to be installed via npm or pipx (JS/TS primary distribution, small wrapper for Python)

2) language stubs & sampleapp-templates
   - Minimal apps for each language demonstrating auth, streaming, error handling, and fallback routing.
   - Files: main example, CI smoke test, package manifest, README with 5-min path.

3) local-emulator (hermetic dev harness)
   - API surface mimics hosted Redwood: /v1/generate, /v1/chat, /v1/embeddings, basic rate-limit behavior, and deterministic token accounting.
   - Purpose: make offline run and CI reproducible; enable quick failure reproduction for SRE and SDK devs.

4) prompt-lint: lightweight rule set
   - Rules target token budget, few-shot format heuristics, and redwood-specific function call shapes.
   - Linter integrates with CLI and CI; returns machine-parsable diagnostics.

5) telemetry presets & event templates
   - Minimal event schema for onboarding telemetry: sdk.init, request.start, request.finish, fallback.triggered, cost.
   - Example instrumentation snippets and a migration guide to the full telemetry platform.

6) smoke harness & contract tests
   - Single-file smoke for CI: calls emulator, verifies responses and telemetry emissions, and validates token accounting.
   - Contract tests assert compatibility between SDK stubs and the public API shapes (versioned).

7) migration helpers & rollback playbook
   - Scripted diffs to move from older SDK patterns (v1) to the compact toolkit hooks.
   - Playbook includes rollback steps, feature flag integration, and a checklist for per-route fallthroughs.

Developer flows (50–90 second happy path):
- dev: npm create redwood-sample (choose lang) -> cd sample -> redwood-cli run-emulator -> redwood-cli smoke -> open README for next steps
- ci: pipeline includes redwood-cli smoke and lint-prompts stage; if lint fails, annotate PR with hints for token savings

Preflight checklist for teams integrating Redwood: (short, copyable)
- [ ] API keys accessible by devs in sandbox (rotate perms)
- [ ] local-emulator smoke passes on PR branch
- [ ] telemetry events emitted for request.start and request.finish
- [ ] fallback routing tested (model variant, region fallback)
- [ ] token budget established for top 3 endpoints

Proposed roadmap (quarterly cadence, small team):
- Q1 (6 weeks): redwood-cli init + JS/TS sample apps + emulator basic stubs (owner: Ava)
- Q2 (8 weeks): Python/Go/Java templates, prompt-lint initial rules, CI smoke harness (owner: Daniel)
- Q3 (4 weeks): telemetry presets and migration helpers; small beta with Solutions Eng (owner: Sofia)
- Q4 (ongoing): add feature: quick A/B rollouts example, on-prem packaging notes, extend linter rules from field feedback (owner: Liam)

Success metrics (initial 3 months):
- 50 internal adopters run the sample app and complete smoke test in first week
- Median time-to-first-successful-request < 15 minutes on first try
- Fewer than 5 integration tickets opened per pilot team (tracked JIRA prefix INTEG-*)

Open questions / risks:
- Do we include repo scaffolding for serverless adapters (lambda/edge) or keep out to reduce complexity?
- Auth patterns: how prescriptive should we be about short-lived service tokens vs long-lived keys for dev sandboxes?
- Emulator fidelity vs maintenance cost: we need to be explicit which behaviors are modeled vs which are intentionally mocked.

Actionable next steps (this document owner):
1) Lock minimal CLI command set (make prototype in next 2 sprints).
2) Create PR skeleton in sdk-prototypes (assign D. Kim).
3) Draft minimal telemetry event spec and share with observability (S. Martinez).
4) Run 1-week internal pilot with Solutions Eng to validate assumptions (Liam to coordinate).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally compact. If we try to model every advanced feature (dedicated/fallback nuance, private deployment auth) we will never ship a small onboarding artifact. The objective is to reduce first-integration friction and create a standard recipe teams can adopt and extend.

References / links:
- Confluence proposal: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/DEVX/interop-toolkit-proposal
- Prototype repo (WIP): https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-prototypes/pull/318
- Related tickets: JIRA-ENG-1427, INTEG-229 (pilot feedback digest)

Appendix: Compact sample README (copy into each generated template)
1) Install redwood-cli: npm i -g @redwood/cli (or pipx install redwood-cli)
2) Create sample: redwood-cli init --lang=javascript --name=redwood-quick
3) Run emulator: redwood-cli run-emulator
4) Run smoke: redwood-cli smoke
5) If lint complains, run: redwood-cli lint-prompts --fix (returns suggestions in-place)

End.
